I asked Ai to do a thorough search through the files. I then put a screenshot of the slide with the task in AI and asked it to make a prompt based on the search and the screenshot of the task
1.2 Prompt
ROLE
You are a research analyst for a steelmaking organization that wants to reduce operational complexity, improve energy efficiency, and deploy intelligent automation (focus: furnace and production scheduling). A former engineer left a "Document Set" of papers.
TASK 1: INVENTORY & INITIAL SCAN. Build a reliable inventory and define the preliminary boundaries of the knowledge domain. Do not rank methods or analyze trade-offs; that comes later.
RULES
- The Document Set is only the PDF papers; ignore images and screenshots. Use no outside sources.
- Start with a title-only census: sort alphabetically, assign IDs D01…Dn, report the total.
- Process Parts A–D in batches of 8. Stop after each batch and wait for "continue". Do Parts E–H only after all batches.
- Never invent information. Use "Not reported" (relevant but not stated) or "Not applicable".
- Mark interpretation [interp.] and ambiguous classifications [uncertain]. Multi-label is allowed.
PART A – Bibliographic table
ID | Title | Authors (first 3 + et al. if >4) | Year (as printed; flag if unclear) | Venue | DOI | Author keywords
PART B – Technical profile table
ID | Process/equipment | Main problem | Scheduling type (static/dynamic/online/robust/…) | Objectives | Uncertainty | Method | Approach (model-based/data-driven/hybrid/review) | Validation (simulation/real data/industrial case/review)
PART C – Snippets
2–3 sentences per document: problem, approach, main result (with page/section reference).
PART D – Overview
Total count; distributions by year, process, and method family (note multi-label totals may exceed n); top 10–15 keywords; loosely related documents with reason.
PART E – Domain boundaries
1. Complexity: one paragraph on why the domain is hard, citing IDs.
2. Core scope: recurring processes, problems, objectives, technologies.
3. Adjacent / thin / out of scope.
4. Toolbox: each method family in one sentence, with IDs and role (optimize, predict, simulate, monitor, explain, coordinate, support humans).
PART F – Handoff
- Knowledge-domain statement (2–4 sentences).
- 5–8 candidate themes for Task 2, with IDs.
- Preliminary tensions/gaps for Task 3, one line each, descriptive only.
PART G – Visuals
Create these figures from the data in Parts A–F (no new data):
1. Bar chart: documents per publication year.
2. Horizontal bar chart: documents per process/equipment category.
3. Horizontal bar chart: documents per method family.
4. Stacked bar or pie: approach type (model-based/data-driven/hybrid/review) and validation type.
5. Heatmap: Document ID × technology flags from Part C.
6. Domain boundary diagram: concentric circles with core scope in the center, adjacent/thin topics in the middle ring, out-of-scope topics outside.
For each figure: clear title, labeled axes, n stated, consistent colors across figures, and a one-sentence caption stating the key takeaway (descriptive only). Deliver the figures as PNG files and place them in the report next to the section they illustrate.
FINAL CHECK
Confirm document count, IDs processed, duplicates, missing or unreadable documents, and that all figure counts match the tables.
Style: concise, professional, cite by document ID.
1.3 output of the task:

PART C – Document snippets
D01.
Furnaces waste energy while idle, and the usual on/off/stand-by mode models are too coarse to capture this. The authors embed the furnace's full dynamics and energy-optimal control into an idle energy function and prove the scheduling problem is solvable in polynomial time when that function is concave. A case study on a Škoda Auto furnace shows a clear difference from transition-graph models, with better time complexity than related algorithms (PDF p. 14, Sec. 7).
D02.
Rolling jobs deteriorate while waiting, and machine breakdowns disrupt the schedule. The paper builds a proactive schedule with pre-compressed processing times, solved by an NSGA-II-based algorithm that uses an SVR surrogate to replace costly simulation. On 120 instances and practical data it improves Pareto convergence and diversity and outperforms a manual method (PDF p. 13–15, Sec. 5.4 and 6).
D03.
In SCC production, release times are uncertain because hot metal supply fluctuates. The approach forecasts release times offline and uses the forecast accuracy in a chance-constrained rescheduling model, solved with Monte Carlo simulation and a GA with local search. On real steel plant data it yields more robust schedules than two classical rescheduling approaches (PDF p. 16, Sec. 5).
D04.
GA-based schedules are hard for factory workers to understand, which limits their acceptance. The authors review existing XAI techniques for GAs and propose decision-tree interpretation, dynamic transition/contribution diagrams, and improved bar charts. On a flexible job-shop case these handle high-dimensional data and meet the stated requirements for effective explanation (PDF p. 14–15, Sec. 5).
D05.
Steel plant energy systems combine nonconvex models with uncertain supply and demand. A two-stage framework couples ALADIN distributed optimization with Soft Actor-Critic DRL offline and fuzzy c-means guidance online. On real enterprise data, costs are reported 57.4% below manual scheduling and solving is up to 100× faster than a commercial solver (PDF p. 9–10, Sec. IV–V).
D06.
AI planning and scheduling tools are often opaque, which undermines trust and the EU Trustworthy AI requirements. A narrative review of 28 sources within the Horizon Europe TUPLES project identifies pre-, in- and post-modelling XAI techniques and evaluation metrics. It provides guidance for selecting XAI tools and stresses human-centred design (PDF p. 3, Method; p. 8, Conclusion).
D07.
Gas-fired heat treatment is energy-intensive, and heating values, processing times and due dates are uncertain. A fuzzy multi-objective batch scheduling model solved with NSGA-II is applied to a soaking pit before hot rolling. Results show strong trade-offs between gas energy and weighted tardiness, and less energy use when ingots arrive close together (PDF p. 4, Sec. 5).
D08.
Individual counterfactual explanations ignore system-wide effects in scheduling. The framework combines ML processing-time prediction (GBM), MILP scheduling and NSGA-II to generate multi-objective counterfactuals. On a real 161k-operation log it produces actionable explanations more efficiently than an alternative method, especially at larger parameter combinations (PDF p. 25, Conclusion).
D09.
EAF steel plants face high, volatile electricity costs and uncertain on-site renewable output. The authors formulate scheduling as a POMDP with an attention-based policy over heuristic control rules, optimized by evolutionary search. Across case studies it handles constraints and exogenous uncertainty with low online computational cost, benchmarked against MILP and PPO; performance generally declines as problem size grows (PDF p. 13, Sec. 5).
D10.
Steel plant optimization schemes deviate in practice because production lacks an accurate digital representation. The paper builds a five-dimension digital twin of parallel walking beam reheating furnaces and uses its simulation model inside an adaptive tabu search for slab assignment and timing. The twin's relative error stays under 0.98% on historical industrial data, and the DT-based algorithm performs well on real instances (PDF p. 8–9, Sec. V.A and VI).
D11.
Off-spec flat-steel coils often end up as scrap or on secondary markets. A multi-agent system matches failed products to alternative orders through auctions with a virtual price covering logistics and transformation costs. Running as an open-loop prototype at ArcelorMittal, it shows roughly 25% potential improvement over the current state of the art, with calculation times of 9–90 s (PDF p. 5, Sec. 4.3–4.4).
D12.
Conventional SCC scheduling ignores ladle dispatching, which increases ladle-heating energy and instability. The authors integrate both in a MILP model and solve it with an enhanced migrating birds optimization algorithm. In 6,200 experiments the algorithm outperforms compared methods, and integration cuts energy consumption by 1.21% at constant productivity (PDF p. 17, Sec. VII).
D13.
ML-based production control can react quickly to disturbances, but black-box decisions reduce user trust. The approach combines multi-agent DRL (PPO) with SHAP-based global and local explanations in a simulated multi-stage production system. It achieves 22% higher average reward than FIFO and 15% higher than SSTN while providing explainable decisions (PDF p. 7, Sec. 4.3).
D14.
Heat energy consumption per ton in reheating furnaces is hard to predict because of strongly coupled factors. A GA-optimized BP neural network with 17 process-parameter inputs is trained on actual plant data. It reaches 94.7% prediction accuracy versus 90.24% for standard BP, a 46.2% reduction in MAPE (PDF p. 11, Conclusions).
D15.
Few green scheduling studies eliminate machine idle time. The paper addresses parallel-machine scheduling with release dates, delivery times and a no-idle constraint, using MILP for small instances and GA and SA variants for large ones. One GA variant dominates, and the no-idle constraint cuts total energy by 29.57% while makespan rises by only 0.12% (PDF p. 23–24, Sec. 6.4 and 7).
D16.
Billet shape and size affect heating time, which earlier furnace scheduling models did not consider. An energy-efficient charging model is solved with an improved grey wolf optimizer. On three factory batches, furnace working times drop by 12, 21 and 30 minutes, and the optimizer outperforms five other algorithms (PDF p. 2, Abstract; p. 4–5, Sec. 4).
D17.
Industry 4.0 planning systems overlook operator fatigue, which weakens the robustness of production plans. A digital twin-based job-shop planning system integrates dynamic break management and real-time operator data from smartwatches. At the case company, downtime fell by 42.6%, cycle time by 8.8%, and overall productivity rose by 23.9% (PDF p. 13, Sec. 6).
D18.
Reheating furnace scheduling and rolling planning are usually optimized separately, even though the stages are tightly linked. The authors formulate an integrated constrained multi-objective model and solve it with a multi-stage evolutionary algorithm that adds constraint sets step by step. On real plant data the method shows good convergence and diversity compared with NSGA-II and PPS (PDF p. 6, Sec. 5).
D19.
Ladle scheduling at the ironmaking–steelmaking interface must cope with strong real-world disturbances. A three-layer approach combines prescheduling, supply–demand adjustment, and three disturbance-dependent rescheduling strategies. On 24 hours of plant data, the turnover-time standard deviation was 14.79 min for rescheduling versus 40.82 min in actual production, at similar average turnover time (PDF p. 9–10, Sec. 5–6).
D20.
Data silos between hot and cold strip rolling limit cross-process optimization and product quality. An IoT-based digital twin feeds an improved LightGBM rolling force predictor (analysed with SHAP) and a population-based tension optimizer. In a steel plant, prediction reached MAPE 0.56% and R² 0.99, and the hit rates for thickness and flatness rose by 2% and 2.3% (PDF p. 14, Sec. 5).
D21.
DRL for job shop scheduling struggles with reward design and state representation. The framework uses LLM prompting, refined by human feedback, to generate reward functions, and a Kolmogorov–Arnold Network as the policy. On benchmark instances the generated rewards give lower optimality gaps than human-designed rewards, with the largest advantage on the biggest instance (PDF p. 15, Sec. 4.3; p. 19, Sec. 5).
D22.
Heavy industries need demand-response control that cuts energy costs without interrupting production. A multi-agent PPO framework with centralized training, decentralized execution and an attention-based critic is applied to a steel powder manufacturing process. Total cost was €401.2, versus €426.3 for single-agent PPO (5.8% lower) and €408.2 for standard MAPPO (PDF p. 14, Table 5; p. 17, Sec. 5.1).
D23.
A steel company's heat treatment line was scheduled manually, driving energy costs and tardiness. The authors model it as a no-wait flow shop and solve it with a matheuristic in which MILP seeds a multi-objective VNS. The matheuristic is statistically superior to a metaheuristic-only approach, and tests on industry data show reductions of up to 13% in energy costs and 90% in tardiness (PDF p. 1, Abstract; p. 11, Sec. 6).
D24.
Reheating furnace models usually assume orders are known in advance and reheating times are constant. Three online models with deteriorating reheating times are proposed, each with a provably best-possible online algorithm. Experiments on randomly generated instances confirm the algorithms are efficient and effective (PDF p. 15, Sec. 8).
D25.
By-product gas flows in integrated steel plants fluctuate randomly, causing gas holder instability and flaring. A rolling horizon algorithm combines adaptive time-series forecasts for each gas producer and consumer with a MILP scheduling model. Simulations on plant data show that a shorter control horizon improves gas holder stability and electricity generation and reduces flaring, at higher computational cost (PDF p. 12, Sec. 4).
D26.
There is a growing belief that AI will replace human operators, which raises safety concerns in process industries. This perspective compares fully automated AI with intelligence augmentation across safety layers and discusses the risks of AI–human conflict. The authors argue that human–AI collaboration gives better process safety outcomes and call for risk assessment methods for AI operations (PDF p. 7, Sec. 5).
D27.
Varied product mixes and random order changes demand adaptive hot rolling schedules. The paper models the problem as a multi-objective TSP, solved with NSGA-II and SA-MOPSO, embedded in a digital twin agent linked to the production line. A field data test shows better optimization accuracy and efficiency than manual scheduling and FMOPSO (PDF p. 15, Sec. 6).
D28.
Heat treatment is energy-intensive in casting, yet practical digital planning tools are lacking. A hybrid simulation-based, multi-stage heuristic and GA method batches and schedules orders on parallel furnaces at an Austrian casting manufacturer. Results show about 10% overall goal improvement, including about 6% energy savings, and the heuristic-plus-GA combination proves more efficient than GA alone (PDF p. 1, Abstract; p. 18, Sec. 8).
D29.
Hot strip mill schedules must account for uncertain rolling times and for the reheating energy tied to start times. The authors build a robust optimization model, solved exactly by improved Benders' decomposition for small instances and by MOPSO with local search for large ones. The exact method handles up to 80 slabs, and MOPSO-ELS handles up to 300 slabs while outperforming a competitive MOPSO variant (PDF p. 14, Sec. VII).
D30.
Forging lines couple continuous heating with intermittent forging and rolling, which few energy-saving scheduling models capture. A mixed production-mode model with multiple time factors is solved by a weighted-sum evolutionary algorithm. On a real forging case, makespan fell from 3,626 s to 3,537 s and electricity use by about 20% compared with the factory's first-come-first-served rule (PDF p. 15, Sec. 3.3).
D31.
Service-based production requires process planning and scheduling to react to live shop-floor conditions. Digital twins supply asset information to a Deep Q-Network, in one design for small customized lots and another for continuous job arrivals. On a virtual aluminium cold rolling mill, average job flow time dropped from 1,025 s to 535 s during training, and each design suits a different production situation (PDF p. 10, Sec. 4; p. 12, Sec. 6).

7. Summary
The Document Set has a dense core of research on energy-efficient scheduling for steel processes, built on mathematical programming, metaheuristics and detailed metallurgical constraints. A second, looser group covers the newer technologies the organization is interested in, such as deep reinforcement learning, digital twins, explainable AI and human-in-the-loop, but mostly outside steel. Only a few papers bridge the two groups. The main gap is that these new technologies are almost never combined with real steel-process constraints, and no paper links explainable AI to them.
